title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system generated a fake news article impersonating a real finance presenter and a government official to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The article was never published by a legitimate news outlet and never reported any actual interview. This represents a deployment of generative AI outside its intended use, weaponized to create material for investment fraud.

The failure occurred at the point where generated content entered circulation without authentication or source verification. Someone could have caught this by checking whether the supposed interview appeared in actual ABC archives, by contacting the real people named, or by verifying the cryptocurrency platform's licensing status before treating the article as credible. News aggregators and platforms hosting the content could have flagged or removed it through basic fact-checking.

It is not established whether any particular AI system was responsible, what platform distributed the fake article most widely, or how many people lost money to the scam.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake news article circulated online claiming that Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated article, which never actually occurred, exemplifies a rising wave of AI-generated investment scams. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research reveals that scammers increasingly use deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to create convincing but fraudulent investment schemes. The regulator took down 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of most commonly impersonated Australians, followed by politicians like Pauline Hanson and Jacqui Lambie. Finance professionals Alan Kohler and Tom Piotrowski are also frequently impersonated. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, positive reviews, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing. Alan Kohler has called for heavy penalties against platforms hosting such content and the AI systems generating it.
